chapter: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
title: Grand Terrace staff, prices and clientele
summary: Staff, German cook Emil, expensive checks.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Yeah. About how many people worked at the Grand Terrace, would you say? Not counting the show.
You know, the waiters and --
Well, they had at least about ten, twelve waiters. And One or two bus boys. Of course they had a couple of day porters.
Bartenders.
Bartenders. And before cover charge come in. We had a cashier.
You mean, you'd have to pay your money at the door?
At the door.
Did they serve food?
Yeah. Had a very good German cook, Emil. Very good. That's where most of my money went. In the kitchen.
Was the -- I read some place that the clientele was quite mixed, and maybe predominantly white.
Yeah.
Well, it wasn't like the Cotton Club was it, where they didn't want black people to come in? Was it?
No, everybody was welcome.
Was it a pretty high priced place?
In those days, yeah. Well, the biggest check, maybe a deuce of people, you might -- your biggest check would be maybe around $10.00.
That was a lot of money.
That was a lot of money back in them thirties, during the Depression. Mostly policy men and pimps could afford that.
Policy men?
Yeah. Run the policy wheels.
And then there were the gangsters?
Yeah. They started fading out in later years.
Yeah, after Capone got busted.
Yeah.
Went in different directions.
Right.
There's still a lot of them --
There's still a lot of them --
-----in the clubs
Yeah, there's still a lot of them around. But they're in legitimate business.
